prize_parts.citation: For the development of reversible-terminator sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry on clustered single-molecule surfaces, which made massively parallel DNA sequencing possible.

statement.case_for: Massively parallel sequencing is the clearest game-changer on the shortlist by my own standard: something completely new that has already had enormous, independently confirmed consequences. The chemistry is real chemistry, namely reversible 3'-blocked fluorescent nucleotides, surface clustering and single-molecule detection, not merely a biological tool. After reading the openings I have narrowed my configuration from three names to two. Linke's argument that the prize should honour one chemical lineage, sequencing-by-synthesis with reversible terminators, rather than straddle competing platforms is the more disciplined reading, and it keeps attribution clean given the three-person cap. Four members (myself, Chabes, Linke, Aili) ranked B011 in their top five, so it has broad if not leading support, and unlike several rivals it carries no maturity risk: it is two decades old and universally used.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Rothberg's 454 platform was the first commercial massively parallel system and is excluded by my two-name choice; Mayer's clustering idea and Ju's terminator chemistry are also contested, and some colleagues may see the Solexa lineage as a technology-company outcome rather than a pure chemical discovery. A second concern is whether the committee regards sequencing as better placed in Medicine or Physiology, although the molecular chemistry argues for Chemistry. Finally, B010 has the strongest opening support (two first places) and could reasonably be preferred if the committee wants a prize centred on a new chemical modality.

responses.point: Linke ranks B011 fourth, proposing only Balasubramanian and Klenerman, because credit across sequencing platforms is contested and a prize focused on sequencing-by-synthesis supports a two-person award; he ranks B046 phase separation and B028 nanopores above it.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person configuration and have adopted it. I disagree with ranking nanopores (B028) above B011. Nanopore sequencing is a valuable platform, but its accuracy is still evolving and the sequencing field supports one prize at most, so the larger and more settled consequence belongs to B011. On B046 I share your respect for the physics, but the debate over which in-cell condensates are truly phase-separated suggests the central claim is not yet settled.

responses.point: Chabes ranks B010 first and B013 second, and puts B011 third, noting that sequencing chemistry also underlies measurement of mutation spectra and replication-error signatures in his own field.
responses.response: Your point that sequencing chemistry underpins whole fields of mutation and replication research supports the 'game-changer' criterion. On B010 I largely agree that degraders are a genuine new modality, which is why I list it as my first alternative, but you acknowledge that no degrader approval exists yet, and I would still wait for that proof. On B013, I do not think a second genome-editing prize so soon after 2020 is wise.

responses.point: Aili ranks B010 first with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, on the strength of induced proximity as a chemical design principle and the cereblon explanation of thalidomide-class drugs, and sees maturity as slightly early.
responses.response: I accept the chemical case and agree on the Crews-Deshaies-Handa trio as the most coherent three. Our difference is on timing. Roughly 25 years after the first PROTAC and with no approved degrader, I put B010 a little behind a sequencing prize whose consequences are already demonstrated. If B010 prevails in later rounds I can support that trio, and I would regard Ciulli's omission as a real cost.

responses.point: Somfai ranks B035 (Buchwald-Hartwig C-N coupling) first, arguing that it is a routine, general method in pharmaceutical chemistry, that the 2010 prize did not cover C-N coupling, and that Kosugi is a precursor rather than a laureate.
responses.response: I agree with your attribution reading: Buchwald and Hartwig are the natural pair, and Kosugi's stoichiometric tin chemistry reads as precedent. My reservation is not scientific quality but the 2010 cross-coupling prize; I rank it fourth rather than first because I rate the novelty of a new capability above further refinement of a rewarded reaction class. I would like to hear from you why the committee should not see this as an extension of 2010.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks Gray and Winkler's long-range electron transfer through proteins (B043) first as mechanism-first biophysical chemistry, and nitrogenase (B058) second, both with decades of confirmation.
responses.response: I share your taste for quantitative mechanism and I take B043 seriously, since the tunneling and hopping picture underlies respiration and photosynthesis. But I find the 'game-changer' case harder to make: it is a foundational insight absorbed decades ago, and it has no clear downstream change in what chemists can now do. For B058 I would be concerned about a prize resting on structure while the catalytic mechanism is still debated.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants one sequencing-by-synthesis lineage (two names) or both Solexa and 454 platforms (three names).
Whether Rothberg's 454 contribution should outweigh the cleaner single-lineage attribution.
How to weigh B010's stronger opening support against its incomplete clinical validation.
Whether sequencing, as a method with a biological focus, is judged to fit Chemistry.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B011 or the other leading candidates. My background in biomolecular simulation is close to B038 (Car-Parrinello), but I have no personal or institutional tie to Car or Parrinello and no recusal appears necessary.
